The agent isn't talking longer — on the shared set, guidelines make conversations slightly shorter: lossless trims ~0.3–0.4 turns in both domains (retail 10.59 → 10.16, airline 9.15 → 8.82), and no variant lengthens them. That matters beyond cost: each turn is a sequential LLM round-trip, so fewer turns means lower end-to-end latency — a faster time-to-completion for the customer, not just a cheaper one. The only real price is on the input side — the larger system prompt riding on every LLM call: retail's 292-guideline prompt pushes cost from ~$0.084 to ~$0.139 per conversation, while airline's smaller playbook is cheaper. And in production even that is largely reclaimable with prompt caching, since the guideline block is identical across every call.

So the trade is a favorable one: for a slightly higher input cost (much of it cached away in practice) the agent lands higher accuracy, higher reliability, and lower time-to-completion at once — not the usual quality-for-latency tradeoff, but all three moving the right way together.

Learned guidelines also improve agents using frontier models

So far, we have used an older, non-reasoning model — 

gpt-4.1
. A fair objection is that learned guidelines might have less to add to an agent using a frontier model: maybe they only patch the gaps of a weaker model. So we tested it directly — we reran airline using 
gpt-5.5
for both the agent and guideline extraction, on the same τ²-bench ReAct scaffold, with guidelines re-mined from the agent's own runs. One detail changes with the model: none of the guidelines extracted in this setup reached support ≥ 3 (they top out at support 2), so the high-support core here is sup2 rather than sup3.

Table 5. Held-out airline performance for the 

gpt-5.5
agent across four trials per task.
Airline · 
gpt-5.5
(20 held-out test tasks)		 AccuracyPass^4
baseline (0 guidelines)72.5%55.0%
sup2 (103 guidelines)80.0% (+7.5)70.0% (+15.0)
lossless (146 guidelines)82.5% (+10.0)70.0% (+15.0)

The learned guidelines improve this setup too. On the same held-out test tasks, appending them to the prompt lifts accuracy +10 pts (72.5 → 82.5) and the strict Pass^4 by +15 pts (55.0 → 70.0) — a larger reliability gain than we observed with 

gpt-4.1
on these very tasks (+10 pts), and from a much higher floor. Learning guidelines around the model can improve an agent even when it starts from a stronger base. And where the baseline's reliability swung between reruns, the lossless configuration reproduced exactly — the gain it buys is dependable, not a lucky draw.

ALTK-Evolve tops the leaderboard comparison

Submissions are scored on the full base split (train ∪ test), as τ²-bench requires, and reported at Pass^4. Because that covers the full task set rather than the held-out test split, these figures differ from the test-task numbers reported above. This is where the practical upshot shows up — prompt-level memory carries agents using each base model into, or past, current frontier company:

  • Retail: #1. On the base split the agent with learned guidelines reaches Pass^4 = 67.5%, ahead of every frontier model and ahead of RAFT-30B-A3B (61.4%), a model fine-tuned on synthetic τ²-bench retail data. Using stock 
    gpt-4.1
    and a prompt-appended playbook, it outperforms that fine-tuned system by +6.1 points.
  • Airline: #1 using 
    gpt-5.5
    , #8 using 
    gpt-4.1
    Against the published board, the compact sup3 core gives the agent using 
    gpt-4.1
    Pass^4 = 44% — 8th, beating GPT-5.2 (no reasoning) and nearly matching Claude Sonnet 4.5. Swap in the stronger base and the same approach tops the field outright: the agent using 
    gpt-5.5
    reaches 82.0%, clearing every frontier entry (66–72%).

Figure 3. Pass^4 comparison between ALTK-Evolve runs and the τ²-bench leaderboard snapshot from October 12, 2026.

Same message in both domains: learning guidelines around the model works across different base models — bringing an agent using an older, non-reasoning model into frontier company on retail, and taking an agent using a frontier model to the top on airline.

Agents can improve without weight updates

Fine-tuning a model on a benchmark is expensive, brittle, and doesn't transfer to the next domain. Here, ALTK-Evolve improves a stock agent on a stock model in both domains — and matches or beats a fine-tuned system on retail — using only prompt-level guidelines extracted from the agent's own runs, automatically, without human annotation, and without any test-set leakage.

Links:

  • Prior posts
  • ALTK-Evolve library — https://github.com/AgentToolkit/altk-evolve
  • τ²-bench — https://github.com/sierra-research/tau2-bench
  • Retail leaderboard submission — τ²-bench PR #542
  • Airline leaderboard submission - τ²-bench PR #551

entries.title: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to 

torch_xla
, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to 
"tpu"
, and you're done.

Wait, what's a TPU? 🤔

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

The old way

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (

torch_xla
). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

Enter TorchTPU 🚀

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a 

torch.compile
integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:
pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

The extra index gives you the CPU build of 

torch
. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Your favourite libraries, now on TPU

Transformers

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass 

device_map="tpu"
. That's it.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="tpu", # will load model directly on the TPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
inputs = tokenizer("The future of AI is", return_tensors="pt").to("tpu")
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=64)
print(tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use 

torch.compile
for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Images? Videos? Diffusers paints them on TPUs 🎨

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs 

pipe.to("tpu")
. For deployment, compiled mode adds one 
compile
call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.
import torch
from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline

pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium", dtype=torch.bfloat16
)
pipe.to("tpu")  # eager mode: that's the whole change
# optional: compiled mode
pipe.transformer.compile(backend="tpu", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

image = pipe("a corgi astronaut planting a flag on a pizza moon").images[0]

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a 

TensorParallelConfig
to 
from_pretrained
and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a 
tp_plan
away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

MiniMax-H3 (video + audio) Qwen-Image-2.1
"The fluffy plush Hugging Face mascot from the picture, a round yellow smiling face with rosy cheeks and two little open hands, stands at the prow of an ancient Greek trireme […] Sound of crashing waves, creaking timber, wind in the rigging, distant seagulls, and a low epic orchestral swell." · 1344×768, 5.2 s, 49 steps · 188 s compiled, 262 s eager"A capybara wearing a wizard hat, reading a book by candlelight, oil painting" · 1024×1024, 40 steps · 3.5 s compiled, 8.0 s eager"A neon shop sign that reads 'QWEN IMAGE 2.1', rainy night, reflections on wet pavement" · 2048×2048, 40 steps

Kernels

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

from kernels import get_kernel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS

repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu"
kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version=1, trust_remote_code=[repo_id])
ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register("tokamax_ragged_dot", kernel.experts_forward)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507",
    experts_implementation="tokamax_ragged_dot",
)

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We test it so you don't have to 🧪

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in 

StaticCache
and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Get started

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to 

"tpu"
.

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

entries.title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
entries.content:
LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-GGUF

Text Generation • 3B • Updated • 717k • 387

AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Update on GitHub

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:

A drop-in compatible API

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your 

import
statement:
- import FoundationModels
+ import AnyLanguageModel

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

  • Tool calling works with every provider.
  • Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested 
    @Generable
    types and arrays of them.
  • Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' 

LanguageModel
protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Hosted models, too

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

  • OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs
  • Open Responses, for any provider with a compatible endpoint
  • Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options
  • Google's Gemini API
  • Ollama
  • Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27
  • Hugging Face Inference Providers, and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

let model = OpenAILanguageModel(
    baseURL: URL(string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/")!,
    apiKey: ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["HF_TOKEN"]!,
    model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b",
    apiVariant: .chatCompletions
)

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Open-weight models got better

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

  • Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at 
    Q4_0
    with quantization-aware training.
  • LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at 
    Q4_K_M
    .
  • Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

let model = MLXLanguageModel(modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit")

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

Upgrading to 1.0 

dependencies: [
    .package(
        url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel",
        from: "1.0.0",
        traits: ["MLX"]
    )
]

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

What's next

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

entries.title: MPS in PyTorch 2.15
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

TL;DR

  • FP8 comes to the Mac: store 
    float8_e4m3fn
    values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU!
  • MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing.
  • Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster.
  • More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition.
  • Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB.
  • More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.
  • Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later.
  • A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding.

What this means for you

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

  • Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with 
    torch.compile
    , Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. (More)
  • Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. (More)
  • Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows (reported in ComfyUI). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
  • FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and 
    F.scaled_mm
    multiplies them directly on the GPU. (More)

Contents

Getting started

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu

FP8 comes to MPS

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds 

torch.float8_e4m3fn
tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with 

F.scaled_mm
, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def quantize_fp8(x):
    limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
    return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale

x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)

y = F.scaled_mm(
    x_fp8,
    w_fp8.t(),
    scale_a=x_scale,
    scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    scale_b=w_scale,
    scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
print(y.shape, y.dtype)

Faster language-model decoding

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Linear layers

MPS has had GEMV kernels for 

torch.mm
since 2.14, but 
F.linear
still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to 
F.linear
, so the common 
[1, 1, hidden_size]
decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Mixture-of-experts layers

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)

out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape)  # torch.Size([64, 128])

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with 

torch.compile
, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Linear algebra gets a boost

Complex-valued computations

Working with complex tensors gets easier. 

complex64
LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:
import torch

a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)

lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())

Small matrices and larger solves

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with 

full_matrices=True
, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Convolutions, padding, and training

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

OperationWhat changes in 2.15
conv1d
forward		 Specialized kernels replace MPSGraph, plus an im2col-plus-matmul path for short outputs. Useful for audio and streaming-model shapes.
Constant padding Moves to Metal kernels, fixing runaway driver-memory growth in tiled video VAE decoding (more below).
Reflection and replication padding New Metal implementations that are faster and fix backward correctness.
Out-of-place dropout 
nn.Dropout
and 
F.dropout
now use the existing fused kernel.
Upsampling backward A Metal gather kernel replaces the MPSGraph resize-gradient path.
Channels-last 
conv2d
backward		 Stays on an efficient channels-last path instead of an NCHW graph with costly strided access.

Softmax and reductions

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. 

softmax
and 
log_softmax
 now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a 

[1, 128256]
row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in 

Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers
makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:
Memory metricMPSGraph paddingMetal padding
Current tensor-allocation peak4.422 GiB4.095 GiB
Allocator-reserved peak8.070 GiB8.070 GiB
Total driver-memory peak270.135 GiB8.108 GiB

More control with MPS streams

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. 

torch.mps.Stream
and the 
torch.mps.stream
context manager provide the interface, and 
Tensor.record_stream
 lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

import torch

x = torch.randn(1024, device="mps")
torch.mps.synchronize()
worker = torch.mps.Stream()

with torch.mps.stream(worker):
    y = x.square()
    x.record_stream(worker)

del x
worker.synchronize()
print(y.cpu().shape)

More operations work on MPS

Several more operations now run on MPS: 

torch.frexp
, 
torch.logspace
, 
torch.take
and 
Tensor.put_
, 
torch.heaviside
, 
torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l
 and unsigned-integer comparisons. 

logspace
doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on 

main
and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Faster LLM decoding

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

ModelBeforeAfterChange
LFM2.5-8B-A1B108.8 tokens/s126.0 tokens/s+16%
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B52.9 tokens/s62.8 tokens/s+19%
Qwen3.8-27B12.1 tokens/s12.6 tokens/s+4%

Attention runs entirely on Metal

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

More MPSGraph to Metal migrations

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), 

std_mean
and 
var_mean
 (up to 4× faster) and 
bincount
 have already landed. 

bincount
is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

A smaller install

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks 

libtorch_cpu.dylib
by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Wrapping up

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

What's next for us

  • More MPS: 2.16 will run attention entirely on Metal, and we'll keep moving operations off MPSGraph.
  • torch.compile
    : we're working on getting rid of graph breaks, so more models compile end to end.
  • Your ideas: what else should we work on in PyTorch? If something is slow, missing or broken, on MPS or anywhere else, open an issue on GitHub and let us know.

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

entries.title: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, 

torch.compile
and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with 

pip install torch-neuronx
.

New backend, native interface in HF libraries

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes 

neuron
as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and 
torch.compile
.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Transformers

Inference

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the 

device_map=neuron
argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

import os

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch_neuronx  # noqa: F401
from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig

MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B"
MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024
PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512

dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron")
world_size = dist.get_world_size()

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size),
    device_mesh=DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(world_size))),
).eval()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
if tokenizer.pad_token is None:
    tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
tokenizer.padding_side = "left"

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "The future of AI is"}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    padding=True,
    tokenizer_kwargs={"pad_to_multiple_of": PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE},
    return_tensors="pt",
)

generation_config = GenerationConfig(
    max_new_tokens=128,
    do_sample=False,
    use_cache=True,
    pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
    eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
    cache_implementation="static",
    max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN,
    prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE,
    compile_config=CompileConfig(backend="neuron", fullgraph=False, dynamic=False),
)

with torch.no_grad():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        inputs["input_ids"],
        attention_mask=inputs["attention_mask"],
        generation_config=generation_config,
    )

if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    prompt_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
    print(tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0, prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens=True))

Training

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's 

SFTTrainer
. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.
import os

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig

from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser


def main(script_args, training_args, model_args):
    # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660)
    torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False

    training_args.model_init_kwargs = {
        "revision": model_args.model_revision,
        "trust_remote_code": training_args.trust_remote_code,
        "attn_implementation": model_args.attn_implementation,
        "dtype": model_args.dtype,
        "device_map": None,
    }
    if int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", "1")) > 1:
        # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded
        training_args.model_init_kwargs["distributed_config"] = DistributedConfig(
            tp_size=int(os.environ.get("TP_SIZE", "1")),
            fsdp_size=int(os.environ.get("FSDP_SIZE", "1")),
        )

    # Prepare dataset
    train_dataset = load_dataset(
        script_args.dataset_name,
        name=script_args.dataset_config,
        split=script_args.dataset_train_split,
    )
    # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset.
    train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns(["messages"])

    # Training
    trainer = SFTTrainer(
        model=model_args.model_name_or_path,
        args=training_args,
        train_dataset=train_dataset,
    )

    trainer.train()
    trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir)
    trainer.end()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig))
    script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config()
    main(script_args, training_args, model_args)

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a 

DistributedConfig
with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in 
model_init_kwargs
, 
SFTTrainer
passes it to 
from_pretrained
, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an 
--fsdp
flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

  • Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in 
    torch.compile
    and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes.
  • torch.compile
    on. Passing 
    --torch_compile true
    is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, 
    torch.compile
    detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure.
  • Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with 
    HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1
    .

The command below launches training with 

torchrun
, which starts one process per NeuronCore. 
TP_SIZE
and 
FSDP_SIZE
set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching 
--nproc_per_node
. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.
TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \
    --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
    --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \
    --dataset_train_split train_sft \
    --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \
    --dtype bfloat16 \
    --max_length 2048 \
    --packing true \
    --packing_strategy wrapped \
    --learning_rate 2e-5 \
    --warmup_steps 0.03 \
    --num_train_epochs 1 \
    --logging_steps 2 \
    --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \
    --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \
    --save_only_model true \
    --torch_compile true

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a 

trn2.48xlarge
instance.

Training runs to completion, and 

trainer.save_model
writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Diffusers

Inference

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP
from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig

# Distributed devices initialization
dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron") # TP
dev = torch.neuron.current_device()
mesh = DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(8))) # TP=8

# Pipeline initialization
model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1"
transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained(
    model,
    subfolder="transformer",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP
)
pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    model,
    transformer=transformer,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
pipe.vae.to(dev)
pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

# Image generation
emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt="A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting", device="cpu")  # text encoder stays on CPU
image = pipe(
    prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev),
    prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None,
    height=1024,
    width=1024,
    num_inference_steps=40,
    generator=torch.Generator("cpu").manual_seed(0), # same noise on every rank
).images[0]
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    image.save("out.png")

You can run this piece of code with: 

NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py
.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Kernels

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Acknowledgments

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

entries.title: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale
entries.content:
reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B

Text Generation • 501B • Updated • 3.56k • 191

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

Update on GitHub

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

TL;DR

  • 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token.
  • Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens.
  • Checkpoint formats: BF16, FP8, and NVFP4
  • Reasoning that can stay in context across turns (
    preserve_thinking
    ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max".
  • Response template in the tokenizer.
  • Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2
  • Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles.
  • Ships with a Rust-based custom harness.
  • Apache 2.0.

Build with Beam

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:

  • You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces
  • You could quantize it for your favorite hardware
  • You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem
  • You could build an RL environment with or for Beam
  • You could benchmark Beam and share the results.
  • You could surprise us!

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

What is Beam?

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

Attention

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, 

(1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1
. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

Mixture of Experts

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

Residual Stream

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step 

k
it adds the sublayer output with weight 
1/sqrt(k)
and keeps the existing stream with weight 
sqrt((k-1)/k)
. The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Long Context

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

ContextIf all 52 layers were globalBeam
32K tokens6.5 GiB1.2 GiB
128K tokens26 GiB4.6 GiB
Full context (1M)208 GiB36.08 GiB

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Benchmark Results

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

Beam (BF16)Beam (FP8)Beam (NVFP4)
Agentic Coding / Terminal
DeepSWE v1.143.3%43.0%42.7%
SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard76.5%78.4%78.6%
SWE Bench Pro v166.1%65.9%65.6%
Terminal Bench v2.180.1%78.9%78.2%
SWE Atlas Codebase QnA31.8%32.2%31.4%
SWEBench Multilingual78.3%78.1%77.5%
SWEBench Verified81.6%80.2%80.7%
Reasoning
AIME 202697.7%98.0%97.5%
HLE (no tools)36.0%36.0%34.8%
HLE (with tools)51.1%51.1%51.1%
SciCode49.2%48.3%46.9%
CriPT AA16.3%17.4%15.4%
GPQA Diamond90.6%90.3%89.3%
LiveCodeBench88.3%88.1%87.4%
Tool Calling / Search
AutomationBench - public split only39.338.239.8%
MCP Atlas80.8%81.5%80.5%
Tau3 Banking36.1%36.8%35.4%
BrowseComp w/ context management76.8%76.7%75.6%
DeepSearchQA w/ context management80.5%79.6%81.1%
General Capabilities
AA-LCR78.2%79.4%78.7%
LongBench v267.5%67.6%67.2%
IFBench79.6%80.7%79.2%
AA Omniscience (index) - public split only10.88.89.8

Hardware Requirements

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Inference Support

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Transformers

Install the latest version of transformers.

pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1"

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

from transformers import pipeline

pipe = pipeline(
    "text-generation", model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B", device_map="auto"
)

messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about Python exceptions."}
]
output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens=2000)
output[0]["generated_text"][-1]

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use 

AutoModelForCausalLM
and 
AutoTokenizer
.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype="auto", device_map="auto"
)

Chat 

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You should only answer with a number."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 * 23?"},
]

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    reasoning_effort="medium" # by default
).to(model.device)

input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)

tokenizer.parse_response(
    outputs[0][input_len:], prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0]
)

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. 

parse_response
reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Tool calling

Complete tool-calling example

def get_weather(city: str, unit: str = "celsius"):
    """
    Get the current weather for a city.

    Args:
        city: The city to look up.
        unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit".
    """
    ...

tools = [get_weather]
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?"}
]

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tools=tools,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)

input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1000)

message = tokenizer.parse_response(
    outputs[0][input_len:], prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0], tools=tools
)
message.get("tool_calls")

Pass 

tools
to 
parse_response
as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 
7
could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Multi-GPU and multi-node

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a 

DistributedConfig
:
import os

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B",
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(
        tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]), ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]), tp_plan={}
    ),
)

Launch the script with 

torchrun
across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

vLLM

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \
  --tensor-parallel-size 16 \
  --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }'

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at 

http://localhost:8000/v1
. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

SGLang

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:

python -m sglang.launch_server \
--model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \
--served-model-name beam \
--tp 4 \
--attention-backend trtllm_mha \
--page-size 64 \
--context-length 1048576 \
--mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
--enable-unified-memory \
--speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
--speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \
--speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \
--tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

python -m sglang.launch_server \
--model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8 \
--served-model-name beam \
--tp 8 \
--attention-backend fa3 \
--page-size 64 \
--context-length 1048576 \
--mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
--enable-unified-memory \
--speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
--speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \
--speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \
--tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

Inference Providers

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://router.huggingface.co/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["HF_TOKEN"],
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B:auto",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}],
)

print(completion.choices[0].message)

Inference Endpoints

We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the 

hf
cli like so:
hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --name beam

What we tested

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

CategoryPrompt DescriptionLow reasoning (tokens)High reasoning (tokens)
Multi-step tool callingFulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse.✅ 544 ✅ 811
Long-context retrieval over a code baseDerive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols.🔴 1,613 * ✅ 5,007
Terminal task in a sandboxInspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check.✅ 582 ✅ 1,548
Math reasoning (AIME-style)How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? Give a justification.🟠 829 † ✅ 2,809
Structured outputConvert an out-of-order revision log into strict JSON: merge patches, cancellations, nulls, dates, currencies and totals.✅ 1,040 ✅ 2,088

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

Post-training Beam

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

SFT with TRL

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s 

SFTTrainer
to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

GRPO with Miles

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

WorkloadReference configuration
Inference / eval, BF1616x H200 per engine
Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles)96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated.
LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles)32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout.
Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles)48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam .

python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \
  --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \
  --model-dir /root/models/Beam \
  --data-dir /data/datasets

export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1
export RAY_ADDRESS=http://${MASTER_ADDR}:8265

python scripts/run_beam.py execute \
  --model-dir /root/models/Beam \
  --data-dir /data/datasets \
  --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \
  --num-rollout 100

What happens in a rollout:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add 

--resume
to continue from the last checkpoint. 
execute-colocate
runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Train with LoRA

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

python scripts/run_beam_lora.py execute \
  --model-dir /root/models/Beam \
  --data-dir /data/datasets \
  --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \
  --num-rollout 100

Build with Beam: Demos

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Hey Beam, build a native local MacOS application!

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Build BeamSpeak, a native macOS menu bar dictation app with a compact recording pill and no main window or account.

Use ⌘⇧Space to start and stop microphone recording, showing elapsed time, microphone level, and transcription status. Run speech recognition entirely locally using a Hugging Face model, preferably Parakeet v3 through MLX, and keep the model loaded between recordings. Paste the transcript into the original app if it remains focused and Accessibility permission is granted; otherwise copy it to the clipboard, preserving newer clipboard changes and never pressing Enter. Handle permissions, cancellation, silence, errors, a two-minute recording limit, and temporary audio cleanup. Deliver source code, a runnable BeamSpeak.app, setup instructions, and verification of offline transcription, the physical shortcut, microphone capture, and text delivery.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents?

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Hey Beam, finetune a decision model for my code base!

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Wrapping Up

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

entries.title: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint
entries.content:
ibm-granite/granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc

Automatic Speech Recognition • 0.5B • Updated • 59.4k • 84

Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint

Enterprise Article

Introduced last spring, the Granite Switch project enables a modular approach to model development. Now Granite Switch 4.1 models, armed with a Decision adapter and the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR leaderboard, can move efficiently between natural-language responses, general and specialized decisions, and speech-to-text tasks—all from one hosted endpoint.

Specifically, Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B models are configured to include:

  • A new Decision aLoRA for general-purpose decision-making (e.g. v1/systemone),
  • A specialized Guardian aLoRA that, on average, outperforms Jev 1.13, Microsoft-Decision-1, GPT-Luna-Decisions, and Clef-Flash on safety-related decision tasks, and
  • Granite-Speech-5.0-Turbo-CTC, the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR Leaderboard, embedded for use in transcription tasks.

All three of these technologies (along with the underlying base model) are composed into one model, taking up approximately the same amount of VRAM on a GPU as the base model would by itself. That means more capabilities with fewer GPUs.

And because the Switch adapters were built as cache-efficient Activated LoRAs, the KV cache created from a base model generation can be reused for any subsequent adapter-based decisions. Combined with our team's recent vLLM contributions to speed up low rank adapter inferencing, as well as a co-located ASR encoder, Granite Switch 4.1 models can switch between a chat request and a decision request and a spoken request, with blazing fast speeds.

Check out our Speech-to-Decisions HF space where granite-switch-4.1-8b transcribes audio, generates summaries, screens for harmful content, and tests 15 other user-defined flags—all running on a single endpoint in real time.

Granite Libraries: The OG Decision Models

Decision models aren’t new. Our previous release of Granite Libraries features a repository of specialized “decision model” adapters and other specialized task adapters that can be composed into custom Granite Switch models. And while Jev and other closed decision models focus on generality, we’ve found that many of our specialized granitelib adapters can outperform generalists on specialized classification tasks.

Compare granitelib adapters with generalist decision models when evaluated on specialized classification tasks.

Because adapters share the base model's KV cache, adding specialists alongside a generalist decision adapter costs almost nothing. You get broad coverage from the generalist and higher accuracy from specialists on the tasks you care about.

In a “Race” between Granite-Switch-4.1-30B (frozen base Granite + 4 specialized aLoRAs) and Jev-27B (frozen base Qwen model + 1 generic decision LoRA), Granite-Switch-4.1-30B was able to complete a real world, 5-step RAG workflow much faster than its competitor.

Compose and Extend Your Own Granite Switch Model

Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B are released with “batteries included”. They are Granite Switch models that we compiled with a predefined set of helpful adapters. But you don’t need to use our version. Anyone can compose their own Granite Switch model, mixing and matching adapters from Granite Libraries to best meet their needs.

Moving forward, we see tremendous opportunity for the community to compose and extend Granite Switch models with custom and third party adapters. We plan to release an Adapter SDK for training adapters in Mellea, along side other tutorials and Granite Switch support. These adapters could be specialized classification adapters to augment decision-based workflows or adapters for specialized language tasks. You could even use custom adapters to teach a 3B parameter version of Granite to play the classic game Doom.

Similarly to Jev, our custom 3B parameter Granite Switch model made split second decisions to navigate the Doom game, but was able to do so at 60 - 100 decisions / second, compared to Jev’s reported 10 decisions / second.1 Unlike Jev, this Granite Switch model can also narrate and respond to your questions while it is playing.

Accessible from anywhere

Coming in 8b and 30b sizes, Granite Switch 4.1 can fit wherever your workload runs. The model runs in vllm with a plug-in (see Granite Switch repo below), and has native inference support in 

llama.cpp
and downstream platforms which allows the model to seamlessly swap in for 
/v1/systemone
API calls anywhere they're used, while also servicing traditional chat calls, all with a shared prefix cache.

Resources for Getting Started

  • Granite Switch 4.1 Model Cards
  • Speech-to-Decisions Demo
  • Granite Switch GitHub Repo
  • Original Granite Switch and Granite Libraries Release Blog
  • Create your own aLoRA v LoRA race on Colab.

Footnotes

1 https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev
